newsitem.title: USA: Allegheny Power to buy Pittsburgh utility DQE.
newsitem.headline: Allegheny Power to buy Pittsburgh utility DQE.

text.p: Allegheny Power Systems Inc., an electric utility company serving five eastern states, will acquire Pittsburgh area utility DQE Inc. for $2.6 billion, the companies said Monday.

The company, which will be renamed Allegheny Energy, will have more than 2 million customers, combining the mostly rural operations of Allegheny with the urban-dominated operations of DQE. Its headquarters will be near Hagerstown, Md.
DQE is the parent company of Duquesne Light Co., which has 580,000 customers in an area of 800 square miles in and around Pittsburgh.
Allegheny has 1.4 million customers in parts of Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia and West Virginia.

Under terms of the transaction, DQE shareholders will receive 1.12 shares of Allegheny Power for each share of DQE. Allegheny said it will issue about 86.5 million shares to DQE shareholders, which, based on Friday's closing prices, makes the deal worth $2.6 billion.
Also based on that price, each DQE share would be worth $33.32. Allegheny closed Friday at $29.75 and DQE closed at $27.125, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
In early trading Monday, DQE climbed $2.25 to $29.375 and Allegheny fell 62.5 cents to $29.125.
Alan Noia, chief executive officer of Allegheny Power, will be chairman of the new company, and David Marshal, president of DQE, will be president.

"The rationale for this merger is simple," said Noia. "Together we can achieve even greater success in the new, competitive marketplace. This merger strategically positions Allegheny Energy as a major regional player in the increasingly competitive electric power market."

"This merger is a natural fit," said Marshall. "Allegheny Power is a winter-peaking operation; its low-cost, efficient operations and suburban and rural customer mix fit well with our summer-peaking operation and urban customer base."
The companies said their boards had unanimously approved a definitive merger agreement.

The companies said they expect to achieve merger-related savings of about $1 billion over the next 10 years and utility rates should be less expensive than they would be if the companies remained separate.
Part of the savings would come from an unspecified number of staff reductions, which would be achieved through reduced hiring, attrition and voluntary reductions, the companies said.
The merger is conditioned on approval by shareholders of both companies and by state and federal regulators. The companies said they hope to receive all necessary approvals within 12 to 18 months.
